Wine Gaming - Commonly used terms. (WIP)

This work in progress post will contain commonly used terms related to gaming using Wine. It will be expanded/corrected as necessary and be linked to from a main getting started post in the future. I'm not a Wine-Gaming expert, so there are chances some of the information below is incorrect. Any suggestions or corrections, feel free to PM.

CSMT

Command Stream Multi-threading, a long time set of changes to improve Direct3D performance (WIKI) they were recently incorporated into the WINE Stable branch. CSMT is now enabled by default since Wine 3.3, and can be turned off using winecfg.

CSMT (Deprecated)

While using winecfg with a Wine-Staging release, the Staging tab will have reference to enabling CSMT, but with a (Deprecated) suffix. This is because Wine has now implemented CSMT into the Development and Stable branches, removing the original need for the toggle option. There are discussions taking place on if it should be removed completely, or it's behaviour changed.

DXVK

A relatively new project, which aims to provide a translation layer for DX11 games running in Wine and the Vulkan Graphics API. When enabled, the DX11 .DLL files (DXGI and D3D11) within a prefix are replaced with the DXVK versions, and DX11 calls made by the running application are translated into calls which the Vulkan API can understand. The result so far being that many games which take advantage of the more advanced feature set in DX11, such as the Witcher 3, have seen substantial performance improvements, both in terms of FPS, and in the reductions of graphical glitches due to missing or poorly implemented features. You can access the project's GitHUB page here.

ESYNC

A recent addition to third party improvements, WineEsync aims to bypass the single threaded Wineserver by executing all synchronization operations in "User-Space". Esync is not included in the standard Wine or Wine-Staging releases. If you want to make use of Esync, you'll need to build a version of Wine with Esync included, or look for a pre-compiled package compatible with your distro. Lutris has started offering specific Wine runners with Esync included.

Some games will benefit greatly from using ESync (removing stutter and increasing FPS etc...), while others will see no difference or crash completely. Your millage will vary.

Gallium 9

An old set of patches, Gallium 9 aimed to provide additional performance improvements to games which utilised D3D9 in certain use cases, specifically, when using the Open Source graphics driver. If you are attempting to run a game which has a D3D9 version, and are using an AMD card, it might be worth looking for a version of Wine-Staging which includes the Gallium 9 patches, to see if that improves the performance. The patches can be turned off or on using winecfg.

It should be noted, however, that Mesa has since incorporated many of the improvements these patches included, so turning them on may amount to little more than a placebo nowadays.

Libraries/DLL Overrides

Often when looking up guides on how to get a particular application running, you'll see mention of DLL Overrides being applied, or else, Libraries being overridden. As Wine is attempting to imitate the Windows' runtime environment, that includes imitating the Windows DLL hell. DLLs in Wine come in two states, Built-in or Native. Setting a DLL in winecfg to Built-in, means the application, if it attempts to load that specific DLL, will be presented with the one that the Wine Project have developed to imitate the official DLL found in Windows. If the Wine Project have not yet implemented an imitation DLL, then you will have to use the Native DLL, which is often provided by the application when it installs into the Wineprefix, or else is obtained by the User via other means.

PBA

Some Wine Packages will explicitly mention that they contain PBA patches. These patches aim to allocate dynamic wined3d_buffers from a single persistently mapped buffer. The idea being to provide faster dynamic geometry in Direct3D games. You can read more about PBA from the project's GitHUB page, here.

Wine

A compatibility layer which aims to provide an environment capable of running Windows applications (including games) on Linux and other nix based operating systems. In danger of over simplifying how it works, it imitates the Windows runtime environment and translates Windows system calls into ones which can be understood by *nix based Operating Systems. Wine comes in two officially supported branches: stable and development, with development containing many more features and improvement which are not yet considered reliable enough to be included in the stable branch.

Wine-Staging

When looking to install wine, you will notice other Wine packages in the list. One of these will be Wine-Staging. Staging combines the current release of the Wine Development branch, and incorporates a bunch of improvements and experimental features aimed at either eking out more performance when running applications via Wine, or else testing an experimental fix/feature. Many of these Staging improvement will eventually make their way into the official Wine releases in some form or another.

With the inclusion of CSMT in Wine Development, it is no longer as necessary as it once was to use Wine-Staging to get playable performance out of many D3D11 games, but it is still worth considering, as it contains a bunch of other experimental fixes which could provide you with better performance in certain games/situations.

Wineprefix

A location on disk which contains the imitation Windows Directory Structure (including DLLs), along with any Wine specific configuration settings applied to that specific prefix. Windows applications are installed or otherwise manually placed within a prefix before being executed by Wine.

Winearch

This refers to whether the Prefix is 32 or 64bit. A 64bit only Windows application will require a 64bit Wineprefix in order to function, as a 32bit prefix will imitate a 32bit Windows environment.

Winecfg

Winecfg is a utility which allows for the modification of certain settings applied to a Wineprefix. Winecg can be used to set what OS the prefix should imitate (XP, 7 etc...), as well as turning on or off additional Staging features, if a Staging version of Wine is being used. WINEHQ has a great wiki which explains the various sections and uses of winecfg.

Wineserver

The daemon process that provides to Wine roughly the same services that the Windows kernel provides on Windows. If your instance of Wine crashes or hangs, and terminating the application's .exe process does not put Wine out of its misery, you may need to kill the wineserver process to completely terminate all processes running under that instance of Wine.

Winetricks

A separately program which can be used to manage existing Wineprefixes. Winetricks allows, either via CLI or a GUI, the ability to install additional Windows components inside a Wineprefix, including fonts, as well as launching the other tools useful for managing a Wineprefix, such as winecfg and winereg. Winetricks can also be used to reset a Wineprefix (deleting all installed applications, resetting the registry and reverting other configuration settings to their default values). You can read more about Winetricks from the WineHQ wiki here.

Wine-Mono

Wine's built-in replacement for Microsoft's .NET Framework implementation. Wine-Mono will often need to be installed in a Wineprefix in order for it to successfully launch Windows' applications.
